newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spanish stocks ending 1996 with a bang.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spanish stocks ending 1996 with a bang.

text.p: Spain's stock market set another record closing high on Friday and has chalked up a whopping 40 percent gain for the year, one of the world's top performances for 1996.
Enthusiasm over European Monetary Union, a restrictive 1997 budget, easing inflation and historically low interest rates have all fed the buying frenzy.

The market set consecutive record highs on Thursday and Friday with only two trading days left in the year. The Ibex-35 blue chip index gained more than 3.0 percent in the two-day stretch, peaking at an all-time high of 5188 on Friday.

"We have a low-inflation environment, higher growth than last year and finances are going in the right direction. It's a good scenario for equities," said Mariano Colmenar, head of research at Barclays De Zoette Wedd in Madrid.
Analysts saw steady improvement in inflation, signs of a pickup in consumption and an infusion of liquidity from domestic mutual funds as the driving forces behind the year-end rally.

With interest rates at their historic lows, bonds at lofty levels and a positive economic outlook, mutual funds have been diversifying and slowly shedding their traditional cautious exposure to equities.

In the first nine months of the year, Spanish bonds had outperformed stocks as the fixed-income market demonstrated greater confidence in Spain's chances of qualifying as a founder of the European single currency planned for 1999.
The stock market was more skeptical about EMU and lagged bond gains. Investors saw in the gap an opportunity for further stock rises and rushed in, said Colmenar.
Inflation was flat in November and up 3.2 percent for the year versus a 4.3 percent rise in 1995.
The economy grew 2.2 percent in the third quarter of 1996 while the trend in consumption appeared to be picking up, giving further incentives to buy stocks.
Meanwhile, the Bank of Spain has downshifted dramatically in 1996 with seven interest rate cuts taking the key money market rate from 9.0 percent in January to 6.25 percent by year-end.

"We are not in a speculative spiral in which the prices are unjustified. It makes economic sense," said Juan Cueto, analyst at Ibersecurities. "With actual interest rates and possibly new declines, the stock market continues to offer potential."
The market's impressive performance was also helped by a healthy injection of political stability and fiscal discipline, analysts said.
"Political risks in 1995 did clearly penalise the stock market," said BZW's Colmenar.

The former Socialist government led by Felipe Gonzalez came under enormous pressure in 1995 from ballooning corruption scandals and accusations it ran a "dirty war" against the Basque separatist group ETA.
In a March election this year, Gonzalez was ousted by Conservative Popular Party leader Jose Maria Aznar who made qualifying for EMU and integration into Europe his top priority.
In September, the government put forth an austere budget for 1997, moulded to the Maastricht Treaty convergence criteria for EMU and approved by parliament on Friday.
Markets greeted it with glee.

Good company performances, particularly in the banking, utilities and telecoms sectors, anticipation of increased privatisations and government measures to liberalise key sectors and open them to competition also encouraged investors.
Analysts said they see room for more gains in 1997 but probably a less dramatic 10 to 15 percent rise.
